surveyDefinition.title: Skin Care Products — consumer survey (U.K.)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skincare routine complexity, purchase drivers, and sensitivity to efficacy and sustainability claims.

segments.name: Clinical Efficacy Buyers
segments.description: High-engagement users with multi-step routines, focused on visible results for specific concerns like aging or hyperpigmentation. They prioritize clinically proven ingredients and are willing to pay a premium for efficacy, but are skeptical of overpromising marketing.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Minimalists
segments.description: Low-to-moderate engagement users who prefer short, simple routines with few products. They are driven by sustainability, clean ingredients, and minimal packaging, and are wary of greenwashing. They are willing to pay more for genuinely eco-friendly options.

segments.name: Budget Family
segments.description: Price-sensitive buyers who purchase skincare for themselves and often other household members. They look for multi-purpose, value-for-money products that last long, and are less loyal to brands, switching to save money or when promotions appear.

segments.name: Luxury Anti-Aging Users
segments.description: High-spend, high-engagement users who invest in premium, often luxury, anti-aging products. They are driven by brand prestige, sensory experience, and perceived efficacy, and are less price-sensitive but demand that the product justifies its cost.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Skin Care Products buyers in U.K.. It asks how people use Skin Care Products, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in U.K. who buy or use Skin Care Products for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have purchased at least one skin care product for personal use in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for their own skin care purchases; Ages 18 and older. Excluded: Professional buyers (e.g., dermatology clinics, spas, salons) purchasing for resale or professional use; Individuals purchasing solely as gifts for others; Children under 18.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
respondentBehaviours: Regularly purchases skin care products (e.g., cleansers, moisturizers, serums, sunscreens)
Researches products online, reads reviews, follows influencers or dermatologist recommendations
May have specific skin concerns (acne, aging, sensitivity, hyperpigmentation)
Brand loyal but open to switching for better efficacy or price
Purchases through multiple channels: drugstores, department stores, specialty beauty retailers, e-commerce, subscription boxes
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by mapping each respondent's skincare world—what products they use, their skin concerns, and how elaborate their routine is. It then follows their purchase journey from trigger to decision, capturing where they learn, buy, and how much they spend. Next, it probes their expectations and the trade-offs they make between efficacy, clean ingredients, and price. It closes with satisfaction, unmet needs, and future intentions, allowing the four segments to be distinguished by their routine complexity, decision drivers, and trade-off priorities.

questions.distribution_note: Cleanser and moisturizer are near-universal across all segments; serum and sunscreen are elevated by Clinical Efficacy Buyers and Luxury Anti-Aging Users, while Eco-Conscious Minimalists and Budget Family keep eye cream and masks lower.

questions.text: How would you describe your skin type?
questions.distribution_note: Combination skin is the most common across the panel; sensitive skin is boosted by the Sensitive Skin Sufferer and Eco-Conscious Minimalist segments, while oily skews toward younger and acne-prone respondents.

questions.text: Which skin concerns are you currently trying to address?
questions.distribution_note: Aging concerns are driven by Clinical Efficacy Buyers and Luxury Anti-Aging Users; dryness and dullness are widespread across most segments, while acne is concentrated in younger and acne-prone respondents.

questions.text: How many steps are in your typical skincare routine?

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skincare routine complexity, purchase drivers, and sensitivity to efficacy and sustainability claims.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural (routine complexity and frequency) and jobs-to-be-done (the primary skin concern the product is hired to address). This fits because skincare buyers differ fundamentally in how elaborate their routine is and what they expect the product to achieve—from basic cleansin

segments.name: Clinical Efficacy Buyers
segments.description: High-engagement users with multi-step routines, focused on visible results for specific concerns like aging or hyperpigmentation. They prioritize clinically proven ingredients and are willing to pay a premium for efficacy, but are skeptical of overpromising marketing.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high routine complexity, high spend, and strong preference for clinical claims and dermatologist endorsement over sensory or packaging attributes.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Minimalists
segments.description: Low-to-moderate engagement users who prefer short, simple routines with few products. They are driven by sustainability, clean ingredients, and minimal packaging, and are wary of greenwashing. They are willing to pay more for genuinely eco-friendly options.
segments.hypothesis: They will report low routine complexity, high importance of natural/clean claims and packaging sustainability, and a tendency to switch away from brands with excessive packaging.

segments.name: Budget Family
segments.description: Price-sensitive buyers who purchase skincare for themselves and often other household members. They look for multi-purpose, value-for-money products that last long, and are less loyal to brands, switching to save money or when promotions appear.
segments.hypothesis: They will report moderate routine complexity, high price sensitivity, high importance of value for money and pack size, and frequent switching driven by price.

segments.name: Luxury Anti-Aging Users
segments.description: High-spend, high-engagement users who invest in premium, often luxury, anti-aging products. They are driven by brand prestige, sensory experience, and perceived efficacy, and are less price-sensitive but demand that the product justifies its cost.
segments.hypothesis: They will report high spend, high routine complexity, low price sensitivity, and high importance of brand reputation, texture, and packaging aesthetics.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'bb7' (When choosing between two similar products, which matters most?) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it forces a single priority choice that cleanly separates the four segments: clinical efficacy seekers pick clinically proven ingredients, eco-conscious minimalists pick clean/sustainable ingredients, budget family planners pick price per use, and luxury anti-aging enthusiasts pick brand reputation.
notes: Clinical efficacy seekers are identified by multi-step routines, focus on specific concerns, clinically proven ingredients, and willingness to pay for visible results.
Eco-conscious minimalists are identified by short routines, preference for natural/organic and sustainable packaging, and willingness to pay more for eco-friendly claims.
Budget family planners are identified by price sensitivity, deal-seeking behaviour, and willingness to give up luxury features to save money.
Luxury anti-aging enthusiasts are identified by high spend, focus on aging concerns, premium packaging/sensory experience, and brand prestige.
10 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by mapping each respondent's skincare world—what products they use, their skin concerns, and how elaborate their routine is. It then follows their purchase journey from trigger to decision, capturing where they learn, buy, and how much they spend. Next, it probes their expectations and the trade-offs they make between efficacy, clean ingredients, and price. It closes with satisfaction, unmet needs, and future intentions, allowing the four segments to be distinguished by their routine complexity, decision drivers, and trade-off priorities.
storyline_notes: Replaced generic 'category relationship' beat with a product-format checklist to confirm category entry and capture the breadth of usage.
Added a dedicated 'skin type and concerns' beat early in consumer_profile because it is the core need state driving skincare purchase and usage.
Introduced 'routine complexity' as a key behavioural measure, as it separates high-engagement (Clinical Efficacy Seekers, Luxury Enthusiasts) from low-engagement (Eco-Minimalists) segments.
In buying_behavior, added a 'purchase trigger' beat to capture the moment a need becomes a purchase, which is critical for switching behaviour.
In preferences_expectations, included a trade-off beat to reveal how segments prioritise efficacy, clean ingredients, and price—essential for distinguishing the segments.
Placed spend and value expectation late in their sections, respecting the sensitivity of money questions.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
